title: Sariputta (Sn 4.16)
hookLine: read it: how a monk should live alone without fear
tomorrow: something covers the whole world like a blanket. what is it?

cards: First night alone in a new place. The fridge hums, a pipe knocks, and every creak in the hallway sounds like footsteps. Or the last one in an office after dark, when the motion-sensor lights click off one row at a time.
The final poem of the chapter of eights starts right there. Sariputta, a disciple of the Buddha, asks on behalf of a monk who goes off to an empty place: what fears should he not tremble at?

teach.b: The answer, in Sutta Nipata 4.16, is surprisingly practical. The Buddha doesn't say nothing out there is real. He names five fears, plainly: gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, run-ins with people, and four-footed animals.
A wise person, he says, doesn't tremble at them.
Not because they're imaginary, but because trembling doesn't help. Then he turns to the body, one of the places where fear can land first. Bear sickness and hunger, cold and heat.
Don't steal, don't lie; touch the weak and the strong alike with friendliness. And here's the line that lands closest to home.

teach.h: WHAT WILL I EAT? WHERE WILL I SLEEP?
teach.b: Don't fret: what will I eat, where will I eat, I slept badly, where will I sleep tonight? Have a sense of measure in food and clothes, and be content. Live simply, and a lot of fear has nowhere to stand.
That's the gift for an ordinary week. Fearlessness here isn't a feeling you wait for.

It's built out of small, steady things: needs kept few, conduct kept clean, kindness given to strong and weak alike. The poem closes the chapter of eights, and it closes not on a grand idea but on a quiet way to live.
Sariputta asked how to be alone without fear. The answer is a way of living lightly enough that fear can't get much of a grip.

how: Forest monks in the Theravada tradition live and meditate in quiet, remote places, and this poem is one of the teachings read on how to live there: few needs, clean conduct, and steadiness in the face of fear.

o: a village where the chapter of eights was first sung
a king who gave the Buddha a park to teach in
a disciple who asked how to live alone without fear

s: the poem says the dangers of being alone are all in your head
it names five real ones, snakes and mosquitoes among them, and says a wise person doesn't tremble at them.
the poem ties fearlessness to living simply: few needs, a sense of measure
don't fret about what you'll eat or where you'll sleep; be content.

games.q: you're moving into your first apartment and can't sleep, running lists of everything that could go wrong. what does Sariputta's poem point you toward?
o: name the real worries, keep needs simple, and let the fretting about tonight go.
stay up until every possible danger has a plan, then you'll be safe.
decide none of it is real, since fear is only ever in the mind.
games.why: the poem names real fears without trembling at them, and then says: don't fret about where you'll sleep tonight. keep a measure, and be content.

practice: Choose one hour later today and make a small plan for it. First, what you'd like that hour to be: simple, unhurried. Then the one thing most likely to crowd it, a phone, a worry, a pile of chores.
Then one plain move for when it shows up. Hold the plan in mind as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sariputta: a disciple of the Buddha, named in the poem, whose plain question about living alone gives the last poem of the chapter of eights its name.

orig.note: Pali: fear, danger. The poem names five bhaya a wise one doesn't tremble at.

carryVoice: A line for the quiet hours: without fear, because there isn't much left to grab. The chapter of eights, read whole.
